# Normal Distribution and Central Limit Theorem {#sec-normal-distribution-central-limit-theorem}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Keywords:** normal distribution, central limit theorem, 68-95-99.7 rule
:::

In the last chapter we measured the standard error of the mean: 3.3. We said it was about the estimator rather than about the students, and left it there. This chapter is about what has to be true before a number like that can tell us anything.

## A standard error is not a percentage {#sec-not-a-percentage}

Here is a question it ought to answer. Our 20 students averaged 70.80. Suppose a colleague draws a different 20 from the same year and gets 74. Is that a normal amount of disagreement between two samples, or did one of us get unlucky?

We know the estimates scatter by about 3.3 points, so a gap of 3 between two of them does not look alarming. But "does not look alarming" is not an answer. We would like to say how often two samples disagree by that much.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(68)

population = np.clip(np.round(rng.normal(70, 12, 10_000)), 0, 100)
our_sample = rng.choice(population, 20, replace=False)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-shape-matters
#| fig-cap: "Two sets of estimates with the same standard error of 3.3. The left is what we have been seeing. The right is what we would have if estimates were arranged differently."
rng_shape = np.random.default_rng(7)

SE, TRUTH = 3.3, 70.0

crowded = rng_shape.normal(TRUTH, SE, 5_000)
half_width = SE * np.sqrt(3)
even = rng_shape.uniform(TRUTH - half_width, TRUTH + half_width, 5_000)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, estimates, title in [(axes[0], crowded, "Crowded in the middle"),
                             (axes[1], even, "Spread evenly")]:
    inside = np.mean(np.abs(estimates - TRUTH) <= SE)
    ax.hist(estimates, bins=45, color="#adb5bd", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)
    ax.axvspan(TRUTH - SE, TRUTH + SE, color="#ffe3e3", zorder=0)
    ax.axvline(TRUTH, color="#c92a2a", linewidth=1.6, zorder=4)
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\n{inside:.0%} inside the band", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("Estimate")
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)

plt.show()

print(f"Standard error, left:  {crowded.std(ddof=1):.1f}")
print(f"Standard error, right: {even.std(ddof=1):.1f}")
```

The standard error by itself cannot get us there. Look at @fig-shape-matters. Both sets of estimates have a standard error of 3.3 and both are centered on the truth, but the red band catches 68% of them on the left and only 57% on the right. Same standard error, different percentage, because the estimates are arranged differently inside it.

But what if estimates always came out bell-shaped, like the left panel?

## Three strange year groups {#sec-three-strange-years}

Here are three more exams, taken by year groups of the same size. None of them behaves like our statistics exam.

```{python}
#| label: odd-populations
rng_shapes = np.random.default_rng(1859)

# A test that separates nobody: scores land anywhere between 0 and 100.
flat = np.round(rng_shapes.uniform(0, 100, 10_000))

# A test that is far too easy: nearly everyone near the top of the scale, a tail below.
easy = np.clip(np.round(100 - rng_shapes.exponential(9, 10_000)), 0, 100)

# A test you either prepared for or did not: two clumps, little in between.
split = np.clip(np.round(np.concatenate([rng_shapes.normal(38, 7, 5_000),
                                         rng_shapes.normal(82, 7, 5_000)])), 0, 100)

for name, scores in [("Flat", flat), ("Easy", easy), ("Split", split)]:
    print(f"{name:6s} mean {scores.mean():6.2f}   sd {scores.std():6.2f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-three-populations
#| fig-cap: "Three year groups, none of them hump-shaped. 10,000 students in each."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.2), sharey=True)
panels = [(flat, "Flat exam"), (easy, "Easy exam"), (split, "Split exam")]

for ax, (scores, title) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.hist(scores, bins=range(0, 102, 2), color="#adb5bd",
            edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)
    ax.axvline(scores.mean(), color="#c92a2a", linewidth=1.6, zorder=4)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlabel("Score")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

axes[0].set_ylabel("Number of students")
plt.show()
```

Nothing in @fig-three-populations resembles our year group.

Now draw 20 students from each, take the average, and do it 5,000 times.

```{python}
#| label: sample-means-three
def sample_means(scores, n, generator, repeats=5_000):
    """Draw n students, take their mean, repeat."""
    picked = np.array([generator.choice(scores.size, n, replace=False)
                       for _ in range(repeats)])
    return scores[picked].mean(axis=1)

flat_means = sample_means(flat, 20, rng_shapes)
easy_means = sample_means(easy, 20, rng_shapes)
split_means = sample_means(split, 20, rng_shapes)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-three-means
#| fig-cap: "Means of 20 students, drawn 5,000 times from each of the three year groups above. Whatever the students looked like, their averages do not."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.2))
panels = [(flat_means, "Flat exam"),
          (easy_means, "Easy exam"),
          (split_means, "Split exam")]

for ax, (means, title) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.hist(means, bins=50, color="#adb5bd", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)
    ax.axvline(means.mean(), color="#c92a2a", linewidth=1.6, zorder=4)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlabel("Mean of 20 students")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

axes[0].set_ylabel("Number of samples")
plt.show()
```

Somehow the original shapes have not carried over into the averages! Now they all look like the left panel of @fig-shape-matters. The averages are bell-shaped, even when the populations were not. The bell-shaped histogram is called the **normal distribution**.


## How large is large enough? {#sec-how-large}

Not every average is normal, though. Think about what an individual score is: it is the average of a sample of size 1. So look back at the easy exam in @fig-three-populations, the one jammed against the top of the scale with a tail trailing left. That is what averages look like when $n = 1$, and nothing about it is bell-shaped. At 20 it was. So somewhere in between the shape changed, and we can infer that the distribution of averages approaches a normal distribution as the sample size gets larger. Let's see how.

```{python}
#| label: fig-n-sweep
#| fig-cap: "Averages from the easy exam at eight sample sizes. Each panel is 5,000 draws. The lopsidedness inherited from the population fades as the samples grow."
sizes = [1, 2, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 100]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(11, 5))

for ax, n in zip(axes.ravel(), sizes):
    means = easy if n == 1 else sample_means(easy, n, rng_shapes)
    ax.hist(means, bins=45, color="#adb5bd", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)
    ax.set_title(f"n = {n}", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

At $n = 2$ the averages are still dragged hard to the left. By 10 the tail is thinner, by 20 it is faint, and from 30 onwards the panels are hard to tell apart from a bell.

The convention sits at 30, and you will see it quoted everywhere as the point at which a sample counts as large. 

Which means the 20 students we have been using all along are, technically, not quite large enough. However, we happen to know our year group is bell-shaped, because we built it that way, so 20 was never going to cause us trouble.

Treat the 30 as a rule of thumb rather than a threshold. Nothing happens at 30 that did not happen at 29. Plenty of real research runs on fewer than 30 subjects, for reasons of cost, access or ethics.

The fact that the distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution as the sample size gets larger, whatever the shape of the original population, is called the **central limit theorem**.

This is why the normal distribution is everywhere in statistics, and it is not because measurements are usually normal. Incomes trail off to the right or reaction times cannot go below zero. The normal distribution turns up because we spend our time looking at averages, and averages go normal even when the things being averaged do not.


## 68, 95, 99.7 {#sec-68-95-997}

So the shape of the sample means is settled. It is normal aka bell shaped. And the normal distribution comes with fixed proportions attached. A given number of standard deviations either side of the center always captures the same fraction of the whole, no matter what is being measured.

For a distribution of sample means, that standard deviation is called the standard error instead. It is $11.94 / \sqrt{20} = 2.67$ points.

We can compute that only because we invented the 10,000 students and can look up $\sigma$. A real study cannot. It would have to build a standard error out of its own sample's spread: for our 20 students that is $14.87 / \sqrt{20} = 3.33$, and it would come out differently for every sample. One clear picture needs one fixed width, so we borrow the true mean and the true standard deviation here.

Mark out three bands either side of the true mean: 2.67 points wide, then 5.34, then 8.01. Then count how many of the 5,000 estimates fall inside each.

```{python}
#| label: coverage
rng_sim = np.random.default_rng(2024)
means_20 = sample_means(population, 20, rng_sim)

se = population.std() / np.sqrt(20)
truth = population.mean()

for k in [1, 2, 3]:
    inside = np.mean(np.abs(means_20 - truth) <= k * se)
    print(f"Within {k} standard error{'s' if k > 1 else ' '} "
          f"({k * se:5.2f} points): {inside:6.1%}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bands
#| fig-cap: "The 5,000 sample means from chapter 2, with bands at 1, 2 and 3 standard errors either side of the true mean."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.hist(means_20, bins=60, color="#adb5bd", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)

for k, shade in [(3, "#f1f3f5"), (2, "#e9ecef"), (1, "#dee2e6")]:
    ax.axvspan(truth - k * se, truth + k * se, color=shade, zorder=0)

ax.axvline(truth, color="#c92a2a", linewidth=1.8, zorder=4)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean of 20 students")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of samples")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

Around 68%, 95% and 99.7%. Those three numbers are worth memorizing.

So a standard error of 2.67 means this: about two thirds of the time a sample of 20 lands within 2.67 points of the truth, and about 95 times in 100, within 5.34.

And that was the second thing we borrowed. The width came from $\sigma$. The centering came from $\mu$: every band in @fig-bands was drawn around 69.99.

A real study has neither. It has one sample, one mean, and one $s$. The next chapter starts there.
